The word squire has several distinct meanings. They are connected by a common thread — someone who holds a position of importance or service.
1. A Knight's Personal Assistant and Apprentice (Medieval — the most common meaning)

This is the most well-known meaning of the word, rooted in the world of medieval Europe (roughly 500–1500 AD).

In those times, becoming a knight was not something that happened overnight. It was a long, step-by-step journey that a young boy began at around the age of seven. The journey went like this:

Page → Squire → Knight

A page was a young boy, perhaps 7–10 years old, who began learning basic manners, service, and riding at a nobleman's household.

A squire was the next stage — a young man, typically between 14 and 21, who was directly assigned to serve a specific knight. Think of the squire as the knight's right-hand man and apprentice rolled into one.

What exactly did a squire do?

The squire's job was both practical and educational. On a daily basis, he:

  • Carried and maintained the knight's armor, weapons, and shield
  • Looked after the knight's horses
  • Helped the knight dress in his heavy armor before battle (this alone required skill, since a full suit of armor could weigh over 30 kg)
  • Served the knight at meals
  • Followed the knight into battle, staying close to retrieve fallen weapons or help a wounded knight off the field
  • Learned swordsmanship, horsemanship, and the codes of chivalry (the moral rules knights were expected to live by)

In short, the squire watched, assisted, and learned — every single day — so that one day he would be ready to become a knight himself. If he proved himself worthy, he would be "knighted" in a formal ceremony, usually around the age of 21.

Was a squire important?

Yes, very. A squire was not a lowly servant. He came from a noble or good family, and his position was one of honor. Being chosen as a squire was a privilege. Famous squires from literature include Sancho Panza (who served Don Quixote) and Squire Tuck — characters that reflect how culturally significant this role was.
2. A Country Gentleman and Major Landowner (British — historical and social)

Over time, as knights became less relevant to everyday life, the word squire shifted and took on a broader meaning in Britain.

A squire came to refer to the principal landowner in a rural village or district — the man who owned the most land in the area, and who was therefore the most powerful and respected person in that community.

Imagine a small English village in the 1700s or 1800s. Most people in the village were farmers or craftsmen. But one man owned the vast majority of the land around that village — the fields, the farms, sometimes even the church and the local roads. That man was the squire.

This was not an official government title. It was a social title — a term of respect that the community gave to the most prominent local gentleman. The squire's house was usually the grandest in the area (often called a "manor house" or "hall"), and he was expected to play a leadership role in the community — settling disputes, supporting the local church, and looking after the welfare of the people who lived and worked on his land.

You'll find this type of squire frequently in classic British novels. When authors like Jane Austen or Thomas Hardy refer to "the squire," they almost always mean this wealthy, influential country gentleman.
3. A Justice of the Peace or Local Official (American — historical)

In parts of the United States, especially in older, rural communities, the title squire was given informally to a justice of the peace, a local judge, or sometimes a prominent lawyer.

A justice of the peace was a low-level legal official who could perform marriages, settle minor disputes, and handle small legal matters in a community. Because this person held local authority and was respected, people would call him "squire" as a mark of that respect — similar to how they might say "judge" or "your honor."

This usage is largely old-fashioned today and is mostly found in historical texts or older American literature, but it's important to know so the word doesn't confuse you when you encounter it.
4. A Man Who Escorts a Woman (formal/literary)

In older, more formal English — particularly in literature — a squire could also refer to a man who accompanies, attends to, or escorts a woman at a social occasion. In this sense, the squire acts as a gentleman companion or chaperone.

This meaning connects back to the idea of service and attendance from the medieval squire. Just as the knight's squire attended to him, this type of squire attended to a lady. This usage is quite rare today and mostly appears in historical novels or formal writing.
5. An Informal Term of Address for a Man (British slang)

In British English, particularly in informal or working-class speech, squire is sometimes used as a friendly, slightly old-fashioned way of addressing a man — similar to saying "mate," "sir," "buddy," or "pal."

For example, a market vendor might say: "What can I do for you, squire?"

This usage is lighthearted and familiar. It carries a slight humor because it takes a word that once meant wealth and high status and uses it casually for anyone. This meaning is becoming increasingly rare and is often used humorously or to sound deliberately old-fashioned.

Squire always carries one of two flavors:

Service and rank — A squire serves someone of higher status (the medieval knight's assistant), or holds a respected position that implies duty to a community (the country landowner, the local official).

Social respect — Whether addressing a nobleman or a stranger on the street, calling someone "squire" signals a kind of respectful acknowledgment of their standing or simply of their personhood.

The meaning you're most likely to encounter depends heavily on context. In a book about medieval history or fantasy fiction — it's the knight's apprentice. In a British period drama or classic novel — it's the wealthy country gentleman. In a historical American text — it may be a local judge. And in casual British dialogue — it's just a friendly word for a man.
